screens.title: GRE over IPsec
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why Generic Routing Encapsulation, or GRE, is commonly combined with IPsec to build secure, routable overlays. GRE provides a virtual point-to-point link that can carry multicast, broadcast, and non-IP protocols—things native IPsec cannot support when used alone. IPsec then encrypts the GRE-encapsulated packets, protecting confidentiality and integrity. You will see how a GRE tunnel is created first as a logical interface, then protected with an IPsec profile or crypto map. I will also show configuration examples for two routers, explain the practical importance of adjusting MTU and TCP MSS to avoid fragmentation, and outline a layered troubleshooting approach that isolates physical reachability, GRE state, routing, and IPsec security associations. A concrete scenario we will use is two sites running OSPF over a GRE tunnel that is protected by IKEv2-based IPsec; this is a common pattern for branch-to-hub connectivity. As you progress, watch for the common misconception that IPsec alone can carry multicast routing updates—GRE is the part that enables dynamic routing to function over a VPN. By the end you should be able to design, configure, and troubleshoot GRE over IPsec with attention to MTU and routing behavior.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › GRE over IPsec
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) over IPsec

Use GRE to carry dynamic routing and multicast across an IP network, then secure the GRE packets with IPsec to create an encrypted overlay.

In this lesson

Understand why GRE is required for routing protocols, configure a tunnel interface, attach IPsec, and handle MTU issues.

Coming up

Configuration templates for Hub and Branch, OSPF over tunnel, and a stepwise troubleshooting checklist.

Explore Key Topics
GRE Basics
Encapsulation for multicast and non-IP protocols.
IPsec Binding
Crypto map vs. IPsec profile applied to tunnel.
MTU & MSS
Adjust tunnel MTU and TCP MSS to avoid fragmentation.
These topics will be used together to enable OSPF and other routing protocols over encrypted tunnels while preserving performance and reachability.
Concept Map
GRE builds routable overlay → IPsec encrypts overlay → Adjust MTU to avoid fragmentation.
GRE Tunnel
Encapsulates multicast and broadcast for routing.
IPsec
Provides encryption and integrity for GRE packets.
MTU
Tune MTU and MSS to prevent fragmentation and loss.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why GRE is paired with IPsec, configure a basic GRE tunnel on IOS-XE, attach an IPsec profile or crypto map to secure that tunnel, run dynamic routing protocols across the secure overlay, and troubleshoot common issues such as MTU-related fragmentation. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: understanding the limitation of native IPsec with multicast, hands-on configuration of tunnel interfaces and IPsec profiles, integrating OSPF or EIGRP over the tunnel, and applying a layered troubleshooting approach. For example, you'll configure a tunnel IP from a dedicated /30, set tunnel source and destination, apply an IPsec profile, and verify that OSPF forms adjacency. You will also practice adjusting ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss to prevent fragmentation during large transfers. This chapter is meant to make you operationally ready: you will not only write configuration, you will also validate behavior with show commands and ping tests, and diagnose failures with crypto and MTU-focused debugging.

screens.title: Skills and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This page expands the objectives into verifiable skills and common pitfalls. You will learn to configure a GRE tunnel interface with an address from a dedicated subnet, choose correct tunnel source and destination addresses, and set tunnel mode gre ip. Next, you will attach an IPsec profile or crypto map and understand when each method is appropriate. You will practice enabling OSPF or another routing protocol on the tunnel so routing updates use multicast across the encrypted overlay. Verification skills include using show interface tunnel, show crypto ipsec sa, show ip route ospf, and show ip ospf neighbor. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Skills and Verification

Practical Tasks

  • • Create tunnel interface and assign /30 tunnel IPs for a point-to-point link.
  • • Set tunnel source and destination to the routers' reachable public IP addresses.
  • • Apply crypto ipsec profile directly to tunnel or use crypto map on the physical interface.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Checks & Misconceptions

• Check physical reachability first. No IP connectivity means GRE cannot form.

screens.title: Why GRE is needed with IPsec
screens.narratorSegment: Begin by defining the problem: native IPsec operates by selecting interesting traffic between two endpoints, typically unicast flows identified in an ACL. That design does not carry multicast or broadcast packets, and it cannot encapsulate non-IP protocols. Dynamic routing protocols such as OSPF and EIGRP rely on multicast or broadcast for neighbor discovery and periodic updates. Without GRE, those protocol packets won't traverse a simple IPsec tunnel. GRE is a tunneling protocol that encapsulates a broad set of network layer protocols into a new IP packet, presenting a point-to-point virtual link. This allows the multicast traffic that OSPF needs to be encapsulated in GRE, then routed over the internet or another IPv4 path. A concrete example: two branch routers need OSPF adjacency. With GRE you assign a /30 to the tunnel interfaces and enable OSPF over that link. Then IPsec encrypts the GRE packets, preserving confidentiality. A common misconception is that IPsec will automatically carry all traffic types; in practice, without an outer GRE header, multicast discovery does not match the IPsec interesting-traffic model. Takeaway: GRE provides the routable overlay required for dynamic routing, and IPsec secures that overlay.

keyIdea.title: Definition summary
keyIdea.text: GRE encapsulates multicast and non-IP traffic so dynamic routing can work; IPsec secures the encapsulated packets.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why GRE is needed

The problem GRE solves

IPsec selects traffic by ACLs and generally supports unicast. It does not transport multicast or broadcast essential for routing protocols. GRE encapsulates those packets inside an IP header so they can traverse an IP-only path.

Concrete example
Two routers form OSPF adjacency using GRE tunnel addresses on a /30; OSPF's multicast hellos are encapsulated and then encrypted by IPsec.
Common misconception
Assuming IPsec alone will carry multicast is incorrect; GRE provides the multicast-capable virtual link.
Key Takeaway

Use GRE when you need multicast or non-IP protocols across a secure VPN; apply IPsec to secure the GRE payload.

Analogy

Think of GRE as an envelope that can hold many types of letters, including multicast letters; IPsec is the lock on the envelope that keeps it safe during transit.

Supporting bullets
  • • GRE creates a point-to-point tunnel interface that looks like a physical link to routing protocols.
  • • GRE encapsulates packet payloads so they can traverse an IP path unchanged.
  • • IPsec can then encrypt the entire GRE packet to provide confidentiality and integrity.

screens.title: GRE tunnel interface basics
screens.narratorSegment: A GRE tunnel is represented on IOS-XE as a logical Tunnel interface. You assign it an IP address from a small dedicated subnet—commonly a /30 for point-to-point—to make it behave like a physical link. The two critical commands are tunnel source and tunnel destination. The tunnel source is the local interface or public IP that will be used as the outer IP, and the tunnel destination is the remote router's public IP. The command tunnel mode gre ip explicitly sets the encapsulation. In practice you must ensure the source and destination addresses are reachable at the physical layer before the tunnel can come up. A concrete configuration sequence shows interface Tunnel0, the ip address on the tunnel, ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss tuning, then tunnel source and destination followed by tunnel mode gre ip. A common error is setting the tunnel source to an interface that is not the egress interface used to reach the peer; this causes the tunnel to fail to establish. Key takeaway: treat the tunnel interface like any other point-to-point link—assign addresses, adjust MTU, and confirm reachability.

keyIdea.title: Tunnel interface
keyIdea.text: Tunnel interface acts like a serial link for routing; source and destination must be reachable and correctly specified.

content.html:
Definition › GRE Tunnel Interface

Create the tunnel

Assign a /30 to the tunnel for a point-to-point link, set source and destination to public addresses, and set tunnel mode gre ip so routing protocols can run over it.

interface Tunnel0
 ip address 10.255.255.1 255.255.255.252
 ip mtu 1400
 ip tcp adjust-mss 1360
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/1
 tunnel destination 203.0.113.2
 tunnel mode gre ip
Explainer bullets
  • • The tunnel IP is used by routing protocols as the peer address for adjacency.
  • • ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss help prevent fragmentation after GRE and IPsec overhead are added.
  • • Ensure the tunnel source selection matches the actual egress used to reach the peer to avoid asymmetric routing problems.
Key Takeaway

Configure the tunnel like a physical P2P link, and tune MTU/MSS early to avoid later performance issues.

screens.title: IPsec binding methods
screens.narratorSegment: When protecting GRE with IPsec on IOS-XE you have two principal methods. The traditional approach is a crypto map applied to the physical outbound interface carrying the GRE outer packets. You define transform-sets, peer, and interesting-traffic ACLs that permit the tunnel endpoints' public IPs; the crypto map matches traffic and applies IPsec to the GRE packet. The modern approach, recommended with IKEv2, is to create an IPsec profile and apply it directly to the tunnel interface. The profile references the transform-set and an IKEv2 profile so the security association is tightly coupled to the logical tunnel. A concrete contrast: using crypto map requires careful ACLs that reference the tunnel endpoints so GRE packets are matched; using an ipsec profile applied to the tunnel interface directly secures the logical link and is cleaner operationally. A common misconception is believing one method always outperforms the other—performance is similar; the operational clarity and flexibility of IPsec profiles, especially with IKEv2 features, is the usual reason to prefer profiles. Key takeaway: choose ipsec profile when available for clarity; use crypto map when legacy constraints require it.

keyIdea.text: IPsec profiles applied to the tunnel are cleaner with IKEv2; crypto maps are the traditional, interface-applied method and rely on ACLs to match GRE endpoint traffic.

content.html:
Comparison › Crypto Map vs IPsec Profile
Crypto Map (traditional)
Applied to the physical interface. Requires an interesting-traffic ACL that matches GRE endpoint addresses. Works with older IKE versions and legacy deployments.
  • • Define transform-set and crypto map.
  • • Apply crypto map to physical outbound interface.
  • • ACL must permit traffic between tunnel source and destination.
IPsec Profile (recommended)
Apply the crypto ipsec profile to the tunnel interface, link it to an IKEv2 profile and transform-set. Cleaner mapping between logical tunnel and security.
  • • Create crypto ipsec profile referencing transform-set and IKEv2 profile.
  • • Apply the profile on the tunnel interface.
  • • Avoid ACL trickiness; ties security to the logical interface.
Practical note

If you use IKEv2, prefer an ipsec profile on the tunnel for cleaner configuration and easier troubleshooting. If constrained by legacy gear, use crypto maps and ensure ACLs match tunnel endpoints.

screens.title: Configure GRE then secure it
screens.narratorSegment: When you configure GRE over IPsec, follow a reliable sequence. Step one: verify basic IP connectivity between the public addresses you intend to use as tunnel source and destination. Without this there is no path for GRE or IPsec. Step two: configure the tunnel interface on both routers, assign the /30 addresses, set tunnel mode gre ip, and tune ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss. Step three: configure your IPsec elements—either create a crypto map and ACL that matches tunnel endpoint addresses or define an IPsec profile that references IKEv2 and the transform-set. Step four: apply the security to the appropriate object (crypto map on the physical interface or ipsec profile on the tunnel). Step five: enable a dynamic routing protocol like OSPF on the tunnel interface and advertise internal networks. Step six: verify using show interface tunnel, show ip ospf neighbor, show ip route ospf, and show crypto ipsec sa. A common mistake is skipping MTU tuning which results in fragmentation and poor performance even when the tunnel and SAs are up. The checklist approach isolates errors and leads to faster root cause identification.

keyIdea.text: Sequence: verify reachability, configure tunnel, secure tunnel, enable routing, verify SAs and adjacency, tune MTU/MSS as needed.

content.html:
Process Flow › Configure GRE then IPsec
  1. Verify IP reachability between public IPs with ping and traceroute.
  2. Configure tunnel interface with /30, tunnel source/destination, and tunnel mode gre ip.
  3. Tune ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss on the tunnel to prevent fragmentation.
  4. Secure the GRE tunnel with an ipsec profile or crypto map and appropriate transform-set.
  5. Enable OSPF or another routing protocol on the tunnel and advertise internal networks.
  6. Verify show interface tunnel, show ip ospf neighbor, show crypto ipsec sa.
Example verification commands
• show interface tunnel 0 — check tunnel state and MTU.
• show ip ospf neighbor — confirm adjacency over the tunnel.
• show crypto ipsec sa — validate SAs are established and packets are encrypted.
Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence to avoid chasing symptoms: reachability, tunnel, security, routing, verify, tune.

screens.title: Example GRE and IPsec profile
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concise, mirrored configuration for a Hub and Branch. The example assumes IKEv2 and IPsec profiles are already defined as in prior chapters. On the hub we create a transform-set, an ipsec profile that links the IKEv2 profile, and a Tunnel0 with a 10.255.255.1/30 address. We set ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss to reduce fragmentation, then specify the physical interface as the tunnel source and the branch public IP as the destination. The branch mirrors these steps. The important operational points are that the ip address on the tunnel forms the OSPF adjacency, the tunnel source/destination must be reachable at the public IPs, and the ipsec profile applied to the tunnel secures GRE packets as they exit and enter. A common mistake is omitting the ip tcp adjust-mss; without it, TCP sessions may negotiate a segment size that causes fragmentation after GRE plus IPsec overhead. Key takeaway: the configuration is short but precise—tuning and peer reachability are as important as the commands themselves. Example GRE and IPsec profile means mirror gre and ipsec profile configs on both ends, tune mtu/mss, and ensure ikev2 profiles match peer identities.. In practical terms, hub and branch configurations (concise, mirrored). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Code Walkthrough › Hub / Branch Templates
Router A — Hub (excerpt)
crypto ipsec transform-set COHORTIA_TRANSFORM esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac

crypto ipsec profile COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE
 set transform-set COHORTIA_TRANSFORM

 set pfs group 14

interface Tunnel0

 tunnel destination 203.0.113.2

router ospf 1
 network 10.255.255.0 0.0.0.3 area 0

Router B — Branch (excerpt)

interface Tunnel0

screens.title: Routing protocols over GRE/IPsec
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic routing over GRE/IPsec uses the tunnel interface as the adjacency point. Configure OSPF on the tunnel by adding the tunnel network to the OSPF process and advertise local internal networks on each router. The OSPF hello and LSAs are encapsulated by GRE and then encrypted by IPsec, allowing the routers to discover each other as if on a physical P2P link. A concrete example: add the 10.255.255.0/30 tunnel network to OSPF area 0 on both ends and verify adjacency with show ip ospf neighbor. If adjacency does not form, first confirm tunnel reachability with ping to the remote tunnel IP, then confirm that IPsec SAs are established and not filtering the GRE packets. A common mistake is not including the tunnel interface in the routing process or expecting routing updates to flow without a tunnel IP assignment. Key takeaway: routing protocols treat the tunnel like any other interface, so think in terms of interface addresses and neighbor formation rather than the physical public addresses. Routing protocols over GRE/IPsec means enable routing on tunnel interfaces and verify adjacency and learned routes; ospf hellos are preserved by gre then protected by ipsec.. In practical terms, enable ospf (or eigrp) on the tunnel, advertise networks, and confirm adjacency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process › Routing over GRE/IPsec

Enable OSPF

Add the tunnel network and local internal networks to OSPF on each router so routes flow over the tunnel.

• Example: router ospf 1 then network 10.255.255.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 and local internal networks.
• Verify adjacency: show ip ospf neighbor.
• Verify learned routes: show ip route ospf.
Troubleshooting hints
  • • If adjacency fails, ping the remote tunnel IP to confirm GRE is up.
  • • If GRE is up but OSPF fails, check IPsec SAs and interesting-traffic ACLs when using crypto maps.
  • • Confirm that OSPF is enabled on the tunnel interface, not only on the physical.
Key Takeaway

Treat the tunnel as the OSPF adjacency link. GRE carries the protocol; IPsec secures it—both must be functioning for routing to work.

screens.title: MTU and TCP MSS tuning
screens.narratorSegment: MTU considerations are critical when GRE is nested inside IPsec. GRE adds header overhead; IPsec adds ESP headers and possibly an IV and ESP trailer. The sum of these additions can cause packets to exceed the physical path MTU—often 1500 bytes on Ethernet—and lead to fragmentation. Fragmentation can cause performance degradation and even packet loss for some protocols. The practical remedy is to reduce the ip mtu on the tunnel interface to a safe value such as 1400 or 1420, and then set ip tcp adjust-mss to a slightly smaller number, for example 1360 or 1380, so TCP peers negotiate smaller segments that fit after encapsulation. A concrete scenario: a host behind R1 sends 1500-byte packets; after GRE and IPsec headers the packet exceeds 1500, gets fragmented on the path, and TCP experiences retransmissions. By lowering tunnel MTU and MSS, segmentation occurs before encapsulation and avoids fragmentation on the physical link. A common misconception is to only change the physical interface MTU; the correct place to tune is the logical tunnel interface and the MSS adjustment for TCP. Key takeaway: tune tunnel ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss proactively to avoid subtle performance faults.

keyIdea.title: MTU insight
keyIdea.text: Lower the tunnel MTU and adjust MSS so encapsulated packets fit within the underlying path without fragmentation.

content.html:
Definition › MTU & MSS Tuning

Why it matters

GRE plus IPsec increases packet size. If the encapsulated packet exceeds the underlying path MTU, it will be fragmented, causing retransmits and poor throughput.

• Recommended starting values: ip mtu 1400 and ip tcp adjust-mss 1360 on the tunnel interface.
• Measure and adjust upward if your path supports larger sizes without fragmentation.
Example scenario
A 1500-byte TCP payload becomes larger after GRE and IPsec headers. Lowering the tunnel MTU ensures routers fragment or segment at the right layer so encapsulated packets do not exceed the path MTU.
Common mistake

Only changing the physical interface MTU is insufficient. Tune the tunnel MTU and the TCP MSS negotiation on the tunnel interface to prevent end-to-end fragmentation.

screens.title: Layered troubleshooting approach
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting GRE over IPsec is best done in layers. Start at the physical and IP layer: verify that the tunnel source and destination public addresses are reachable with ping. If they are not, fix basic routing or firewall issues first. Next, check the GRE tunnel with show interface tunnel and ping the remote tunnel IP; if the tunnel is down, re-check tunnel source/destination and reachability. If the tunnel is up but routing fails, verify routing configuration and OSPF neighbor state with show ip ospf neighbor and show ip route. If routing is correct but traffic is not secure or SAs are missing, inspect show crypto ipsec sa and show crypto ikev2 sa; debug crypto can be used carefully. For suspected fragmentation, use debug ip icmp to find 'Fragmentation needed' messages and test with reduced MTU. A concrete diagnostic flow: reachability → tunnel state → routing adjacency → IPsec SA validation → MTU checks. A common misconception is to jump directly to crypto debug; instead, verify simple reachability first. Key takeaway: methodical layering reduces noise and points you to the correct corrective action faster.

content.html:
Troubleshooting › Layered approach

Diagnostic flow

  1. Confirm IP reachability between tunnel endpoints (ping/traceroute).
  2. Check GRE tunnel state and ping remote tunnel IP.
  3. Verify routing and OSPF adjacency.
  4. Validate IPsec SAs and peer state.
  5. Investigate MTU-related fragmentation if performance issues persist.
Quick commands
• ping to public peer
• show interface tunnel 0
• show ip ospf neighbor
• show crypto ipsec sa
• debug ip icmp (for fragmentation clues)

screens.narratorSegment: This guided lab follows the hands-on activity provided in the chapter. You have R1 (Hub) with public 198.51.100.1 and internal 192.168.1.0/24, and R2 (Branch) with public 203.0.113.2 and internal 10.0.0.0/24. Use a dedicated /30, 10.255.255.0/30, for tunnel addresses. Steps: ensure IKEv2 and IPsec profiles exist on both routers as in earlier chapters. On R1 configure interface Tunnel0 with 10.255.255.1/30, ip mtu 1400, ip tcp adjust-mss 1360, tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/1 and tunnel destination 203.0.113.2, set tunnel mode gre ip and apply crypto ipsec profile COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE. content.html:
Lab Walkthrough › Configure and Verify

Stepwise checklist

  1. Ensure IKEv2 and COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE are on both routers.
  2. Configure Tunnel0 on R1 and R2 with /30 tunnel IPs and MTU/MSS tuning.
  3. Apply crypto ipsec profile to the tunnel interface.
  4. Enable OSPF on the tunnel and advertise internal networks.
  5. Verify adjacency and SAs, then ping internal hosts.

Starter template (R1 hub)

interface Tunnel0
 ip address 10.255.255.1 255.255.255.252
 ip mtu 1400
 ip tcp adjust-mss 1360
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/1
 tunnel destination 203.0.113.2
 tunnel mode gre ip
 crypto ipsec profile COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE

router ospf 1
 network 10.255.255.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
Key Takeaway

Perform and verify each stage of the lab: reachability, tunnel creation, IPsec binding, routing, and end-to-end tests—address MTU early.

Scenario A

GRE and IPsec SAs are up, but large file transfers experience drops and retransmits. Likely cause: MTU/MSS mismatch leading to fragmentation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why Generic Routing Encapsulation, or GRE, is commonly combined with IPsec to build secure, routable overlays. GRE provides a virtual point-to-point link that can carry multicast, broadcast, and non-IP protocols—things native IPsec cannot support when used alone. IPsec then encrypts the GRE-encapsulated packets, protecting confidentiality and integrity. You will see how a GRE tunnel is created first as a logical interface, then protected with an IPsec profile or crypto map. I will also show configuration examples for two routers, explain the practical importance of adjusting MTU and TCP MSS to avoid fragmentation, and outline a layered troubleshooting approach that isolates physical reachability, GRE state, routing, and IPsec security associations. A concrete scenario we will use is two sites running OSPF over a GRE tunnel that is protected by IKEv2-based IPsec; this is a common pattern for branch-to-hub connectivity. As you progress, watch for the common misconception that IPsec alone can carry multicast routing updates—GRE is the part that enables dynamic routing to function over a VPN. By the end you should be able to design, configure, and troubleshoot GRE over IPsec with attention to MTU and routing behavior.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why GRE is paired with IPsec, configure a basic GRE tunnel on IOS-XE, attach an IPsec profile or crypto map to secure that tunnel, run dynamic routing protocols across the secure overlay, and troubleshoot common issues such as MTU-related fragmentation. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: understanding the limitation of native IPsec with multicast, hands-on configuration of tunnel interfaces and IPsec profiles, integrating OSPF or EIGRP over the tunnel, and applying a layered troubleshooting approach. For example, you'll configure a tunnel IP from a dedicated /30, set tunnel source and destination, apply an IPsec profile, and verify that OSPF forms adjacency. You will also practice adjusting ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss to prevent fragmentation during large transfers. This chapter is meant to make you operationally ready: you will not only write configuration, you will also validate behavior with show commands and ping tests, and diagnose failures with crypto and MTU-focused debugging.

This page expands the objectives into verifiable skills and common pitfalls. You will learn to configure a GRE tunnel interface with an address from a dedicated subnet, choose correct tunnel source and destination addresses, and set tunnel mode gre ip. Next, you will attach an IPsec profile or crypto map and understand when each method is appropriate. You will practice enabling OSPF or another routing protocol on the tunnel so routing updates use multicast across the encrypted overlay. Verification skills include using show interface tunnel, show crypto ipsec sa, show ip route ospf, and show ip ospf neighbor. A frequent misconception is assuming that IPsec alone will allow OSPF adjacency; if you rely on IPsec without a GRE wrapper, multicast discovery will not traverse the VPN. Another trap is forgetting to tune MTU and TCP MSS, which can silently degrade performance. These verification steps and checks are the milestones you should reach before considering a deployment complete.

Begin by defining the problem: native IPsec operates by selecting interesting traffic between two endpoints, typically unicast flows identified in an ACL. That design does not carry multicast or broadcast packets, and it cannot encapsulate non-IP protocols. Dynamic routing protocols such as OSPF and EIGRP rely on multicast or broadcast for neighbor discovery and periodic updates. Without GRE, those protocol packets won't traverse a simple IPsec tunnel. GRE is a tunneling protocol that encapsulates a broad set of network layer protocols into a new IP packet, presenting a point-to-point virtual link. This allows the multicast traffic that OSPF needs to be encapsulated in GRE, then routed over the internet or another IPv4 path. A concrete example: two branch routers need OSPF adjacency. With GRE you assign a /30 to the tunnel interfaces and enable OSPF over that link. Then IPsec encrypts the GRE packets, preserving confidentiality. A common misconception is that IPsec will automatically carry all traffic types; in practice, without an outer GRE header, multicast discovery does not match the IPsec interesting-traffic model. Takeaway: GRE provides the routable overlay required for dynamic routing, and IPsec secures that overlay.

A GRE tunnel is represented on IOS-XE as a logical Tunnel interface. You assign it an IP address from a small dedicated subnet—commonly a /30 for point-to-point—to make it behave like a physical link. The two critical commands are tunnel source and tunnel destination. The tunnel source is the local interface or public IP that will be used as the outer IP, and the tunnel destination is the remote router's public IP. The command tunnel mode gre ip explicitly sets the encapsulation. In practice you must ensure the source and destination addresses are reachable at the physical layer before the tunnel can come up. A concrete configuration sequence shows interface Tunnel0, the ip address on the tunnel, ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss tuning, then tunnel source and destination followed by tunnel mode gre ip. A common error is setting the tunnel source to an interface that is not the egress interface used to reach the peer; this causes the tunnel to fail to establish. Key takeaway: treat the tunnel interface like any other point-to-point link—assign addresses, adjust MTU, and confirm reachability.

When protecting GRE with IPsec on IOS-XE you have two principal methods. The traditional approach is a crypto map applied to the physical outbound interface carrying the GRE outer packets. You define transform-sets, peer, and interesting-traffic ACLs that permit the tunnel endpoints' public IPs; the crypto map matches traffic and applies IPsec to the GRE packet. The modern approach, recommended with IKEv2, is to create an IPsec profile and apply it directly to the tunnel interface. The profile references the transform-set and an IKEv2 profile so the security association is tightly coupled to the logical tunnel. A concrete contrast: using crypto map requires careful ACLs that reference the tunnel endpoints so GRE packets are matched; using an ipsec profile applied to the tunnel interface directly secures the logical link and is cleaner operationally. A common misconception is believing one method always outperforms the other—performance is similar; the operational clarity and flexibility of IPsec profiles, especially with IKEv2 features, is the usual reason to prefer profiles. Key takeaway: choose ipsec profile when available for clarity; use crypto map when legacy constraints require it.

When you configure GRE over IPsec, follow a reliable sequence. Step one: verify basic IP connectivity between the public addresses you intend to use as tunnel source and destination. Without this there is no path for GRE or IPsec. Step two: configure the tunnel interface on both routers, assign the /30 addresses, set tunnel mode gre ip, and tune ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss. Step three: configure your IPsec elements—either create a crypto map and ACL that matches tunnel endpoint addresses or define an IPsec profile that references IKEv2 and the transform-set. Step four: apply the security to the appropriate object (crypto map on the physical interface or ipsec profile on the tunnel). Step five: enable a dynamic routing protocol like OSPF on the tunnel interface and advertise internal networks. Step six: verify using show interface tunnel, show ip ospf neighbor, show ip route ospf, and show crypto ipsec sa. A common mistake is skipping MTU tuning which results in fragmentation and poor performance even when the tunnel and SAs are up. The checklist approach isolates errors and leads to faster root cause identification.

Let's walk through a concise, mirrored configuration for a Hub and Branch. The example assumes IKEv2 and IPsec profiles are already defined as in prior chapters. On the hub we create a transform-set, an ipsec profile that links the IKEv2 profile, and a Tunnel0 with a 10.255.255.1/30 address. We set ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss to reduce fragmentation, then specify the physical interface as the tunnel source and the branch public IP as the destination. The branch mirrors these steps. The important operational points are that the ip address on the tunnel forms the OSPF adjacency, the tunnel source/destination must be reachable at the public IPs, and the ipsec profile applied to the tunnel secures GRE packets as they exit and enter. A common mistake is omitting the ip tcp adjust-mss; without it, TCP sessions may negotiate a segment size that causes fragmentation after GRE plus IPsec overhead. Key takeaway: the configuration is short but precise—tuning and peer reachability are as important as the commands themselves. Example GRE and IPsec profile means mirror gre and ipsec profile configs on both ends, tune mtu/mss, and ensure ikev2 profiles match peer identities.. In practical terms, hub and branch configurations (concise, mirrored). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dynamic routing over GRE/IPsec uses the tunnel interface as the adjacency point. Configure OSPF on the tunnel by adding the tunnel network to the OSPF process and advertise local internal networks on each router. The OSPF hello and LSAs are encapsulated by GRE and then encrypted by IPsec, allowing the routers to discover each other as if on a physical P2P link. A concrete example: add the 10.255.255.0/30 tunnel network to OSPF area 0 on both ends and verify adjacency with show ip ospf neighbor. If adjacency does not form, first confirm tunnel reachability with ping to the remote tunnel IP, then confirm that IPsec SAs are established and not filtering the GRE packets. A common mistake is not including the tunnel interface in the routing process or expecting routing updates to flow without a tunnel IP assignment. Key takeaway: routing protocols treat the tunnel like any other interface, so think in terms of interface addresses and neighbor formation rather than the physical public addresses. Routing protocols over GRE/IPsec means enable routing on tunnel interfaces and verify adjacency and learned routes; ospf hellos are preserved by gre then protected by ipsec.. In practical terms, enable ospf (or eigrp) on the tunnel, advertise networks, and confirm adjacency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

MTU considerations are critical when GRE is nested inside IPsec. GRE adds header overhead; IPsec adds ESP headers and possibly an IV and ESP trailer. The sum of these additions can cause packets to exceed the physical path MTU—often 1500 bytes on Ethernet—and lead to fragmentation. Fragmentation can cause performance degradation and even packet loss for some protocols. The practical remedy is to reduce the ip mtu on the tunnel interface to a safe value such as 1400 or 1420, and then set ip tcp adjust-mss to a slightly smaller number, for example 1360 or 1380, so TCP peers negotiate smaller segments that fit after encapsulation. A concrete scenario: a host behind R1 sends 1500-byte packets; after GRE and IPsec headers the packet exceeds 1500, gets fragmented on the path, and TCP experiences retransmissions. By lowering tunnel MTU and MSS, segmentation occurs before encapsulation and avoids fragmentation on the physical link. A common misconception is to only change the physical interface MTU; the correct place to tune is the logical tunnel interface and the MSS adjustment for TCP. Key takeaway: tune tunnel ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss proactively to avoid subtle performance faults.

Troubleshooting GRE over IPsec is best done in layers. Start at the physical and IP layer: verify that the tunnel source and destination public addresses are reachable with ping. These are the essential concepts to remember. GRE encapsulates multicast and non-IP traffic, providing a virtual point-to-point link. GRE over IPsec is an architecture where GRE creates the routable path and IPsec secures the GRE packets, enabling dynamic routing over secure overlays. The tunnel interface is the logical construct you configure, and tunnel source and destination select the public endpoints used to build the outer IP packets.
